Additionally, I have consulted various other relevant sources. 

An offer by law Offer is part of contract negotiations where a party agrees to do or not do something in exchange for consideration. An offer must be stated and delivered in a way that would lead a reasonable person to expect a binding contract to arise from its acceptance. An offer gives the offeree the ability to accept and form an enforceable contract. 

When a valid offer is made, an acceptance by the offeree creates a binding contract. An offeror generally can not retract the offer once the other party has accepted. A court may not find a binding contract regardless, though, if the negotiation did not involve consideration, involves an illusory promise, or if the offeror did not have the capacity to enter into the contract. However, a contract offer can be withdrawn by notification to the offeree of the intent to withdraw the offer before the offeree has accepted. Offerors typically can withdraw an offer before acceptance in any contract negotiation unless the parties have created an enforceable option contract. If the offeree rejects the offer, the offer can no longer be accepted by the offeree. 

An offer can also be made in the form of a counteroffer. The offeree that receives the initial offer can make a new offer of their own instead of accepting the initial offer. This counteroffer acts as a rejection of the initial offer and creates an entirely new offer that can be accepted or rejected. 

Consideration is a promise, performance, or forbearance bargained by a promisor in exchange for their promise. Consideration is the main element of a contract. Without consideration by both parties, a contract can not be enforceable. For instance, if a person used the money to purchase an apple, the apple is the merchants consideration, and the money is the persons consideration. 

Types : Consideration could be a promise, performance, forbearance, or property with legal value, but the economic benefit is not required. 
A gift or gratuitous promise can not be a consideration for they have no bargaining. The past performance also can not be a consideration as there is no exchange. 

Substitute for consideration : A contract without consideration could be enforceable if it has a substitute. Substitutes are promissory estoppel or detrimental reliance under Restatement ( Second ) of Contracts, or good faith modification under UCC. 
Promissory estoppel/detrimental reliance : A contract without consideration is enforceable if the nonperformance of the promisor will cause injustice. Elements of promissory estoppel are ( i ) the promise has reasonable, foreseeable, and detrimental reliance on the promisor, and ( ii ) the enforcement of the promise is necessary to avoid injustice. 
Good faith modification : A modified contract is a kind of new agreement, which changes parties obligations and then requires new consideration. But contract modification made in good faith under UCC is enforceable even without consideration

I am writing to address the response I received regarding my complaint to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) concerning the rejection of my payment coupons by American Express ( AMEX ). After careful review, I maintain that my payment coupons constitute valid negotiable instruments, and their rejection constitutes a breach of AMEXs fiduciary duty, non-compliance with their own SEC filings, and a violation of relevant UCC provisions and federal regulations. 

According to UCC 3-104 ( a ), a negotiable instrument is defined as an unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed amount of money, with or without interest or other charges described in the promise or order, if it : - Is payable to bearer or to order at the time it is issued or first comes into possession of a holder ; - Is payable on demand or at a definite time ; and - Does not state any other undertaking or instruction by the person promising or ordering payment to do any act in addition to the payment of money. 

The payment coupons I submitted meet the criteria outlined in UCC 3-104 ( a ) and therefore must be recognized as valid negotiable instruments. By rejecting these instruments, AMEX has failed to acknowledge their validity under the UCC. 

Under UCC 3-604 ( a ), a debt is considered discharged if a party tenders payment in good faith and the creditor refuses to accept the payment. My payment coupons, which were properly executed and tendered in good faith, were rejected by AMEX without valid cause. This rejection discharges the debt according to UCC 3-604 ( a ). 

Furthermore, UCC 3-603 ( b ) states that if a negotiable instrument is tendered as payment and rejected, the obligor is relieved of any obligation to pay interest on the amount, and the creditor must return the instrument. Despite my requests, AMEX has failed to return the payment coupons, thereby violating this provision. 

AMEXs actions constitute a breach of fiduciary duty, as the company has an obligation to its customers to honor valid negotiable instruments as a form of payment, in accordance with their own SEC filings. By failing to do so, AMEX has engaged in deceptive practices, misleading me as an investor and customer. 

AMEX 's refusal to accept my valid negotiable instruments as payment, without proper investigation or resolution of the dispute, violates 12 CFR 1026.12 and 1026.13. These regulations require AMEX to promptly investigate and resolve billing errors, including disputes over the validity of payment instruments. AMEXs failure to address the core issue of my right to redeem the negotiable instruments and their reliance on an unsubstantiated claim that the payment coupon is not a valid form of payment violates these consumer protection regulations. 

Failure to address these issues satisfactorily may result in further legal action, including but not limited to, filing additional complaints with regulatory bodies and pursuing legal remedies for breach of fiduciary duty, deceptive practices, and violations of federal law.

Legal Obligations and Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) Violations Under the FCRA, American Express has specific obligations to ensure that disputed information is not reported as negative or delinquent until the dispute is resolved. Additionally, under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ), creditors are required to report accurate information to credit reporting agencies and must promptly correct any inaccuracies. 

Further, under Section 611 ( a ) of the FCRA ( 15 U.S.C. 1681i ), I have the right to dispute inaccurate information on my credit report directly with the credit reporting agencies. American Express is also required to investigate my dispute thoroughly and provide me with the results of that investigation. The law also requires that if the dispute is not resolved in my favor, American Express must allow me to submit a statement of my perspective to be included in my credit report. 

Moreover, under the Fair Credit Billing Act ( FCBA ), I am entitled to protection against unauthorized or incorrect charges. The law prohibits creditors from continuing to report a disputed charge as delinquent or negative while an investigation is still pending.

As a result if you paid your account in full but made other charges during the month, the minimum payment would still be deducted. 

In XXXX, Citi began reducing the minimum payment for any payments received. As a result if you made any payment over the minimum payment amount, the minimum payment would not be taken out of your account.

I did not read any notices about this change in automatic payment practices although I acknowledge that Citi may have sent communication.

This happened to be {$41.00} each month. When I received the statements for each month ( attached ) they showed that the balance subject to interest rate was for an amount significantly higher than my minimum payment amount.

I was contacted by Chase Bank by letter that they had determined that my condominium address is in a flood zone, and therefore, I must buy flood insurance to protect their interest in the condo unit. Oddly, they also wrote that FEMA determined my home was in a flood zone.

If I did not purchase flood insurance for them, they would do so for me and pass the costs on to me by raising my mortgage. They then wrote that if I believe I'm not in a flood zone, to contact FEMA and to request an amendment or revision to the flood map ( XXXX or XXXX ) and that I would have to pay for any costs associated with getting them to revise the map and send proof. I went to the FEMA website, entered my address and it showed that I was NOT in a flood zone as of XX/XX/year>. So I'm not sure what they are supposed to revise or amend. 

I called Chase to get more information and the person I spoke to reiterated that FEMA made this determination. I point her to the FEMA website and she said she was not sure how to read the map. She asked me to contact FEMA and to go through the XXXX process. 

I called FEMA and the person I spoke to said ( 1 ) that FEMA does not communicate with banks about flood map updates, and ( 2 ) Chase bank has a third party they contract with that makes the " Standard Flood Hazard Determinations '' ... or something like that. This XXXX representative then went to their maps and confirmed that my home is not in a flood zone. I asked XXXX what to do and they recommended doing both of the following actions : ( 1 ) Go through the XXXX process but that it takes 60 days ; ( 2 ) File a complaint with the regulatory body over the organization that Chase contracts with to make the determinations, and to contact the state attorney general. FEMA gave me a number to call. 

I called that number, went through a long menu of option, spoke to someone who then told me that it does sound like Chase is engaged in forced-insurance. She then said the best entity to help me through this is the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau.

I decided to contact Chase one more time. I explained the situation, and relayed to them what FEMA said and that FEMA denies communicating with them directly ( contradicting what the previous Chase representative said ). This new Chase rep admits that it was another entity that makes that determination, and reiterated the only remedy available to me is to fill out the XXXX forms at my expense. She also reiterated that if I don't buy a flood insurance policy for Chase, they would do it for me, and pass the costs to me, even though it'll take 2 months before FEMA can send proof that I'm not in a flood zone. She mentioned something about offering a refund if they were wrong, but that seems to contradict aspects of what is written in the letter, particularly where there's a gap in coverage.

In short, as best as I understand it, Chase contracts with some 3rd Party to make determinations about whether a property is in a flood zone, then Chase claims that it was FEMA who made that determination, then demands homeowners to buy flood insurance to protect Chase 's interest in the property. If the homeowner doesn't comply, Chase will buy what they openly admit may not be the most affordable insurance. To comply with their demand, they give homeowners LESS than the 60 days it takes to go through the XXXX process ( which you may have to pay for ) to prove you are not in the flood zone, even though ANYONE can simply go to the FEMA website, enter their address, and see that they are not in a flood zone.

This is not at all fair.

sub_issue: Delays with the closing process
complaint_what_happened:
Chase Bank offers a 21 day close guarantee on their home mortgage loans. It is something they advertise as buying a home in a competive housing market requires closing escrow quickly. It is something they still advertise right now. While shopping for a mortgage company for my recent home purchase, Chase offered this guarantee on numerous occasion as a means of enticing me as a home mortgage customer. Not only at their website, but relayed directly to me by XXXX separate Chase loan advisors, including the one I ultimately chose. At the time, the closing guarantee was increased from {$5000.00} to {$20000.00}. I decided to go with Chase for my home mortgage loan in large part due to this guarantee, as my situation involved a timely closing due to relocation and my partner starting a new career. My home purchase offer was accepted on XX/XX/XXXX and thus escrow was opened no later than XX/XX/XXXX or XXXX, XXXX. During escrow, my Chase loan advisor assured me that everything was moving on time and we were set to close on XX/XX/XXXX. I completed all my tasks and returned documents quickly as requested. My desired interest rate was XXXX XXXX with XXXX points, which my loan advisor indicated he was confident I could obtain. After numerous counter offers and signficant effort moving more liquid cash into my Chase bank accounts, Chase would not offer me that and I could only obtain XXXX XXXX if I bought it down for several XXXX dollars. My loan advisor suggested that I not buy it down and just re-finance later, so he suggeseted I take XXXX XXXX XXXX with XXXX out of pocket and I agreed. A few days before the scheduled close date of XX/XX/XXXX, my closing was delayed to XX/XX/XXXX with no explanation. On XX/XX/XXXX, a member of the Chase team called to arrange for a notary for me to sign lending documents on XX/XX/XXXX at my home, which was a XXXX She assured me that we can sign on XXXX  and everything would close on XXXX  XX/XX/XXXX. She then called back a few minutes later and said there are no notaries that work on XXXX, so it would have to be XXXX XXXXXX/XX/XXXX, but assured me that there's nothing to worry about because Chase will close and fund the loan the same day docs are signed. She set up an appointment for XXXX a.m. on XXXX XX/XX/XXXX to sign documents and I thought all was in order. Come that morning, no one showed up at my house. I tried calling the Chase agent that made the arrangements but she did not answer. I finally got a hold of my Chase loan advisor a few hours later who tried to figure out what was going on. I also called the escrow company, who informed me that they should be the ones arranging a notary for document signing and not Chase and were confused why Chase was doing that, and moreoever, informed me that in XXXX XXXX XXXX, you can not close the same day as document signing because the docs can not be recorded until the next day. This was the first I heard of that rule, and no one at Chase knew about this local rule when they clearly should have. After wasting an entire morning, the escrow company did arrange me to sign docs later that evening on Monday, XX/XX/XXXX, but because it was late, and because Wednesday, XX/XX/XXXX was the XXXX holiday, we did not close until Thursday, XX/XX/XXXX. 
The closing date was critical to me and made this clear to Chase from the beginning, and of course they said no problem and allued to their close guarantee bonus should be there any issues. Well I closed 3 days late but late and no one at Chase accepted responsibility for the delay. I incurred real out of pocket costs for a hotel room as my partner started her new job in XXXX XXXX on XX/XX/XXXX, and what's more it was a very stressful situation without any clear answers or direction from Chase when it was needed most. It was clear to me, the escrow company, and my real estate agent, that Chase was the cause of the delay because of their lack of knowledge regarding the XXXX XXXX recording rule and because they did not stay on top of documents with the escrow company during the critical period days before the scheduled close date. 
Immediately after closing, I asked about the Chase 21 day closing guarantee as this would have gone a long way towards alleviating all the negative feelings resulting from the delayed closing, but all I was told was that all accounts are automatically reviewed post closing, and I would be informed if I qualify in XXXX weeks. Multiple follow-ups led to no answers and more run-around. I did receive calls from XXXX managers at Chase and I explained the entire situation in clear detail. Ultimately, Chase indicated that I did not qualify for the closing guarantee and the initial call that informed me of that decision provided no clarity or reason as to why. I had to ask for a written explanation, which I finally received nearly XXXX weeks later. The letter appears to indicate that I did not qualify because my rate changed from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX  within 10 days of closing. Yet, I only settled for XXXX XXXX at the advice of my Chase XXXX XXXX, who never once indicated that doing so would cause any kind of delay. Furthermore, I only accepted XXXX XXXX  so I wouldn't have to come out of pocket to buy points, despite assurances by Chase - and significant effort moving more liquid cash into my Chase accounts as directed - that I would receive XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX without any buy down. Chase 's written letter also erroneously states that I closed escrow on XX/XX/XXXX - this is incorrect as I closed on XX/XX/XXXX. So not only is their reasoning illogical, their written explanation is erroneous. Chase 's handling of this entire situation has not only been frustrating and costly to me in terms of money and time, but it has been insulting as it is quite Chase had no desire to uphold their 21 day close guarantee bonus. It is deceptive advertising that they use to their advantage. They used it to obtain my business, roped me along despite my ability to obtain a better rate from a smaller local mortgage broker, then made me jump through all sorts of hurdles to pursue the closing guarantee bonus, only to deny it. A simple internet search will review many other customers like me who were deceived by the same marketing ploy. Chase has now gone dark on me on this matter, as I've reached out to my Chase lending advisor 's XXXX since receiving the letter from Chase explaning my denial to see if I could speak to someone else as the agent who relayed the denial by phone was not only insulting but incompetent ( she called me 3 times and every time called me by the wrong first name despite my correcting her every time ), but she did not respond.

Citibank makes it incredibly easy to sign up for checking and or savings account. You can do so online without ever talking to a person. If you want to cancel your account they make it incredibly difficult. There is no way to cancel online. You must call their customer service line. That customer service rep will request you give them your security word. I have no recollection of ever filling out a security word for my account and am usually very good about keeping those sorts of things. A XXXX search suggested that XXXX only has you select a security word for accounts that have credit cards. They also requested my card number, but I was never issued a card for my account ( no debit or credit card ). When I searched online on Citi 's webpage and app, there was no way to look up my security word and when I clicked on a link in their " FAQ '' that said " Forgot Security Word '' the link opened to a page not found notice. 

I asked for assistance and the first customer service person hung up on me. The second one was more helpful ( because I stated I intended to file a complaint with the CFPB ) and stated the only way I could close my account was to go to a branch. I asked her where the closest branch was from my city ( XXXX  XXXX XXXX ), knowing the closest branch was hundreds of miles away. Her supervisor was able to send me a text message to authenticate my identity and then stated he submitted an application to cancel my account. This shows the bank CAN cancel accounts over the phone without a security word or debit card number ( both of which I do not believe ever existed for this account ), but they make it very difficult to do so. Most consumers can not aggressively advocate on their own behalf and had I not been aggressive, they would not have canceled my account- and eventually would have started charging fees on my checking account. There is no way to change or look up the security word and they stated they couldn't issue me a debit card without the security word. As a result, I was going to be forced to drive hundreds of miles to the nearest branch just to close an account. 

I agree with the FTC that it should be as easy to cancel something as it is to sign up for it. The barriers Citi has placed in the way of canceling accounts are intentionally designed to stop people from canceling, so that they can continue to collect fees and keep money in their bank.

Under Title 12 CFR 1026.10 ( a ) ( 3 ), part of the Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), creditors are mandated to promptly credit consumer accounts for payments or other transactions. If a creditor fails to credit a consumers account, it constitutes a significant billing error. This provision ensures that consumers are accurately charged and that payments are correctly applied to their accounts. 

When a creditor fails to credit a payment, it not only impacts the consumer 's financial standing but also may lead to wrongful late fees, damage to credit scores, and undue stress. Under this regulation, consumers have the right to dispute such errors and seek corrections. complaint_what_happened: I am XXXX XXXX and I am a natural person. This is me, the actual person submitting this dispute, not a third party. I am writing to formally request the immediate removal of an erroneous account reported by loan servicer Dept of EdXXXX XXXX account number XXXX from my credit report. Despite my numerous attempts to resolve this issue over the past year through multiple disputes, Dept Ed ( XXXX ) has consistently failed to produce the original promissory note and instrument of indebtedness that validates this alleged debt. According to the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681, credit reporting agencies are required to ensure the accuracy and integrity of the information included in consumer reports. Specifically, under 15 U.S.C. 1681i, credit bureaus must reinvestigate the accuracy of the disputed information, and if the information can not be verified, it must be deleted. XXXX 's inability to provide the necessary documentation to substantiate this debt clearly indicates that this account is unverifiable and thus must be removed. The failure to provide a promissory note and original instrument of indebtedness also contravenes the provisions under the Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), 15 U.S.C. 1601 et seq., which mandates clear documentation and transparency of loan agreements. The absence of these critical documents raises substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the reported debt. Furthermore, the Federal Trade Commission ( FTC ) has repeatedly affirmed in various rulings that credit reporting agencies must delete unverifiable information. In the landmark case of XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX, the court underscored the necessity of credit bureaus conducting a reasonable reinvestigation into disputed debts. The court ruled that failure to perform such an investigation or to correct inaccuracies constitutes a violation of the FCRA. This case sets a clear precedent for the requirement to remove unverifiable accounts, such as the one in question. Moreover, the case of XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX further emphasizes that consumers are entitled to accurate credit reporting and that credit reporting agencies must take action to correct or delete unverifiable information from their reports.

Subject : Complaint Against Navient Corporation and Navient Solutions , LLC for FTC Federal Violation 16 C.F.R. 433.2 Missing from For-Profit Private School Loans Dear CFPB and FTC, I am writing to formally report violations of FTC Federal Regulation 16 C.F.R. 433.2 by Navient Corporation and Navient Solutions , LLC on three separate occasions. 

On XX/XX/year>, I received a School Misconduct Private Loan Discharge Application ( EXHIBIT A ). I completed this application, providing evidence of school misconduct along with federal violations committed by Sallie Mae, now operating as Navient Corporation and Navient Solutions , LLC . This completed application, along with the supporting evidence, was mailed on XX/XX/year>, with a return receipt. 

On XX/XX/year>, I received a notification through my Navient portal confirming receipt of my Private Loan School Misconduct Discharge Application ( EXHIBIT B ). On XX/XX/year>, I received a letter from Navient stating that my School Misconduct Discharge has been approved, and Navient has waived the remaining balances of my private student loans in the amount of {$16000.00} ( EXHIBIT C ). Enclosed with the letter was a check for {$630.00} ( EXHIBIT D ). 

However, Navient has, on three occasions, given, received, enforced, and accepted payments on private loan contracts where the Holder Rule was absent from the promissory notes for these three loans ( EXHIBIT E, pages 4, 5, 6 ). This constitutes a violation of federal law.

The Holder Rule, established by the Federal Trade Commission ( FTC ), requires that a specific notice be included in certain consumer credit contracts, including promissory notes for private student loans. ( EXHIBIT H ). This notice preserves the consumers right to raise claims and defenses against any holder of the loan that they could assert against the original creditor. If this rule is violated, it renders the contract unenforceable or provides the consumer grounds for seeking refunds of payments made under that contract. 

By approving my misconduct application, Navient has admitted that my school engaged in misconduct. However, the check issued to me, covering payments made only since XXXX, is grossly inadequate. I have not cashed this check, as I do not accept a mere {$630.00} after years of payments made on fraudulent contracts and a school proven to have engaged in misconduct. 

In my application, I outlined that Navient is in violation of federal law by accepting payments on three contracts that lack the Holder Rule, as required ( EXHIBIT F, pages 26, 27 ). Navient has had the opportunity to rectify this by issuing full restitution through my School Misconduct Discharge Application. I am entitled to a refund for all payments, including interest ( EXHIBIT G1 and EXHIBIT G2 ), on these three loan contracts that violate federal law. 

Unlike federal student loans, each private student loan contract requires a corresponding promissory note. There is no statute of limitations on the Holder Rule ( EXHIBIT H ). Each violation is subject to a {$50000.00} fine by the FTC. Even if a loan has been paid off but the promissory note did not include the Holder Rule, the contract is unenforceable. 

I am entitled to recover the payments I have made. I have included my application outlining proof of these violations, along with the contracts and promissory notes, for your review. Navient is not entitled to state that their decision on payments is proprietary, especially concerning impactful decisions related to federal violations and individuals ' financial well-being.

I do not see this reflected on the interest amount shown on the Nelnet site. So : if I make a payment to Nelnet, how will that payment be applied? Will they apply it to the interest that should be removed? Have they already changed the interest due amount? Nelnets failure to communicate at any step of the process has caused me unnecessary confusion and stress. Clear, timely and accurate communication is surely a basic responsibility of any functional business. 



During this time, I tried to contact Nelnet numerous times regarding my loans using the form on their contact us page, to try to get more information about my loans. Each time, I received an error message asking me to log in again, which did not resolve the issue. I tried logging in on multiple devices, and at different times on different days. I also tried to call Nelnets international number on XX/XX/XXXX to get more information at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX ( I live overseas. ) After hearing the introduction, Thank you for calling Nelnet, there was no further sound, instruction or signal from their telephone line. The agent also informed me that I had already been approved for the SAVE program. After talking with the agent, I found an email address for Nelnet to report problems with technical issues. The first reply I received was an automotic reply about how to log in when I had forgotten my password and how to update my contact information. I had not had any issues regarding logging in to my account, nor had I reported any, and had just confirmed with the agent that all of my contact information was correct the entire time this ordeal was ongoing. I sent a second email asking to confirm that any IT issues regarding submitted emails via their contact form had been resolved, and that any issues on their side that might prevent them from sending me updates had been resolved. I received a reply that I should talk to a customer service agent regarding any complex issues with my loan - still not an answer to my questions regarding their IT and email system.

In order to find the actual APR that was used to calculate the finance charge as disclosed on the contract, I multiplied the monthly payments as disclosed on the contract ( {$510.00} ) by twelve ( 12 ) months in a year, which gave me the actual yearly total ( {$6200.00} ) based on the monthly payment as disclosed on the contract. I then took the yearly amount ( {$6200.00} ) and divided it by the amount financed as shown on the contract ( {$19000.00} ) for the purpose of calculating what the actual APR was that was applied to get the finance charge as disclosed on the contract, and the total of all payments that would have been paid at the end of six ( 6 ) years. 

After dividing the yearly amount ( {$6200.00} ) by the amount financed ( {$19000.00} ) I then discovered the actual APR ( 31.23337094039 % ) which was applied to the unpaid amount of the amount financed. In order to ensure that my math was correct, I multiplied the actual APR ( 31.23337094039 % ) by the amount financed ( {$19000.00} ) which gave me the same total of yearly payments ( {$6200.00} ) when I multiplied the monthly payments as disclosed on the contract by twelve ( 12 ) months in a year. I then took that yearly amount and multiplied it by six ( 6 ) years because that's how long the term of the contract was. Pursuant to 15 U.S.C. 1606 ( c ) in accordance with the regulations of the CFPB as imposed by The Congress in the Truth in Lending Act ( " TILA '' ), for the purposes of accuracy and compliance with that subchapter, it is a violation for the APR as disclosed to be greater or lesser than 1/8 of one ( 1 ) percentage point from the actual APR. Notice of Intent to Sell Vehicle Within 60 days of repossession and at least 15 days before the sale, the lender must send a notice that includes the following information : The car will be sold after 15 days from the date the notice was mailed or given The amount required to get the car back before the sale The reason why the full amount must be paid The owner 's rights regarding reinstating the loan or redeeming the vehicle Post-Sale Accounting After the sale, the creditor must provide the owner with an accounting that includes the sale price, how the funds were used, and any surplus or deficiency.

This decision is based on significant violations of the Truth in Lending Act ( XXXX ), breach of contract, misrepresentation of warranty coverage, deceptive financing practices, failure to disclose my right to rescission, and the improper inclusion of prohibited fees in the finance charge.

# # # Grounds for Rescission : 1. **Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ) Violation** : - XXXX included tax, tag, title fees, service fees, and registration fees in the finance charge calculation, which is prohibited under 15 U.S.C. 1605 ( a ) and Regulation Z ( 12 CFR Part 1026 ).

2. **Breach of Contract** : - By misrepresenting the finance charges and including prohibited fees, XXXX breached the terms of the contract, making it voidable.

3. **Misrepresentation of Warranty Coverage** : - XXXX limited warranty excluded services that by law should be included, violating the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act ( 15 U.S.C. 2301 et seq. ), the Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ), and the Federal Trade Commission Act ( FTCA ).

4. **Deceptive Financing Practices** : - The retail installment contract was misrepresented as extending credit directly from the dealership. Instead, I was made to pay a third-party finance company, Capital One Auto Finance , without clear disclosure. This practice is deceptive and potentially unlawful under TILA and the FTCA.

5. **Failure to Disclose Right to Rescission** : - CarMax failed to disclose my right to rescind the contract within the legally required period. Under TILA, consumers have a right to rescind certain credit transactions, and failure to disclose this right is a significant violation.

6. **Improper Handling of Down Payment** : - Despite being charged a finance charge, I was made to pay a {$5000.00} down payment in cash. This contradicts the principles outlined in 15 U.S.C. 1605 ( a ). If the finance charge covered all costs associated with financing the vehicle, the requirement of an additional cash down payment constitutes an unfair and deceptive practice. This practice is further supported by case law such as **Rodash v. AIB Mortgage Co. , 16 F.3d 1142 ( 11th Cir. 1994 ) **, which held that the improper inclusion of fees in the finance charge violates TILA.

7. **Misrepresentation and Inclusion of Warranty as Insurance** : - XXXX required me to obtain insurance before I could take possession of the vehicle and falsely represented a limited warranty as insurance, which is illegal. The limited warranty was included in the finance charge, contrary to the requirements of 15 U.S.C. 1605 ( a ). Representing that a warranty offers protections that it does not offer is also illegal under federal laws.

8. **Failure to Disclose Insurance Options** : - XXXX never disclosed that insurance could be offered through them, nor did they disclose the cost of such insurance. According to 15 U.S.C. 1635 ( b ) & ( c ), unless a specific statement in writing is furnished by the creditor to the person to whom credit is extended, setting forth the cost of the insurance, if obtained through or through their creditor, and stating that the person to whom the credit is extended may choose the person through which the insurance is to be obtained, the requirement to obtain insurance without providing these disclosures constitutes a violation. XXXX told me I had to get insurance to drive off the lot, never giving me an option and never offering insurance directly. This failure to disclose is a direct violation of TILA.

9. **Application of 26 CFR 15a.453-1 ( e ) ** : - The regulation pertains to the installment method of reporting income from sales of personal property. XXXX failure to properly disclose the finance charge in the Bill of Sale, while recognizing it in the Retail Installment Contract, violates the transparency required in installment sales and the accuracy of financial reporting.

10. **Discrepancy in Finance Charge Calculation** : - The contract specifies a finance charge of {$12000.00} on an amount financed of {$39000.00} at an APR of 9.23 % over 72 monthly payments of {$720.00}. However, this calculation does not add up correctly. At an APR of 9.23 %, the finance charge over the term of the loan should be significantly lower. This discrepancy further indicates misrepresentation and deceptive financing practices. 

# # # Misrepresentation of Warranty Coverage : The XXXX limited warranty excluded several services that should be included by law, violating the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act ( 15 U.S.C. 2301 et seq. ), the Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ), and the Federal Trade Commission Act ( FTCA ). Specifically, the warranty exclusions that are problematic include : 1. **Preventative Maintenance Services** : - Preventative maintenance services or parts replacement as suggested by the manufacturer in its maintenance schedule should not be excluded under a comprehensive warranty.

2. **Repairs Related to Manufacturer 's Defects** : - Repair or replacement of parts due to manufacturers defects should be covered. Excluding these goes against the implied warranty of merchantability under UCC 2-314 and the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act.

3. **Failures of Covered Parts** : - Property damage arising from the failure of covered parts should also be included in the warranty coverage. The exclusion of these services limits the consumer 's protection and violates the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act and the Federal Trade Commission Act ( FTCA ) .

# # # Legal Support : 1. **Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ) ** : - **15 U.S.C. 1605 ( a ) ** : Defines finance charges and explicitly excludes tax, tag, title fees, service fees, and registration fees from being included in the finance charge.

- **Regulation Z ( 12 CFR Part 1026 ) ** : Outlines the requirements for clear and accurate disclosure of finance charges, prohibiting the inclusion of certain fees.

- **15 U.S.C. 1635** : Grants consumers the right to rescind certain credit transactions, requiring clear disclosure of this right.

- **15 U.S.C. 1635 ( b ) ** : Specifies the effects of rescission, including the return of any money or property given as a down payment.

- **15 U.S.C. 1635 ( c ) ** : States that the consumer 's written acknowledgment of receipt of any disclosures required under this subchapter creates a rebuttable presumption of delivery.

2. **Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act** : - Requires clear and detailed disclosure of warranty terms and prohibits disclaimers or limitations not clearly stated in a single document.

3. **Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ) ** : - **UCC 2-314** : Implied warranty of merchantability ensures goods are fit for ordinary purposes.

- **UCC 2-315** : Implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose applies when a seller knows the particular purpose for which the goods are required and that the buyer is relying on the seller 's skill and judgment to select suitable goods.

4. **Federal Trade Commission Act ( FTCA ) ** : - **15 U.S.C. 45 ( a ) ** : Prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. Misrepresentation of warranty coverage and deceptive financing practices constitute unfair and deceptive practices.

5. **Case Law** : - **Ford Motor Credit Co. v. Milhollin , 444 U.S. 555 ( 1980 ) ** : Emphasizes the importance of clear and accurate disclosure of finance charges under TILA.

- **Rodash v. AIB Mortgage Co. , 16 F.3d 1142 ( 11th Cir. 1994 ) ** : Held that the inclusion of certain fees in the finance charge, which should have been excluded, constituted a violation of TILA.

- **Chrysler Credit Corp. v. Whitney , 51 Ohio St.3d 75, 554 N.E.2d 1163 ( 1990 ) ** : Addressed the improper inclusion of fees in the finance charge.

- **Santos-Rodriguez v. Doral Mortgage Corp. , 135 F.3d 28 ( 1st Cir. 1998 ) ** : Highlighted the significance of accurate finance charge disclosures and the impact of including improper fees.

sub_issue: Problem with fees charged
complaint_what_happened:
Ally is systemically improperly charging a disposition fee to customers who turn in appreciated vehicles on lease to dealers. Here are the facts and analysis of my case : Re : Lease Agreement 10 AF -671-MI-e 10/18 ( Lease ) Dear Sir or Madam : Ally is demanding payment of a Disposition Fee of {$390.00} plus sales tax pursuant to the above-referenced Lease ( copy attached ). As explained below, I have no obligation to pay the Disposition Fee because the vehicle was purchased from Ally under my purchase option.

I ask that Ally withdraw its claim and remove any adverse information that it has posted to my credit report in connection with the Lease. I assume that I am not the only Ally customer who has been improperly charged this disposition fee and I am presenting my claim to class action attorneys and also registering a complaint with CFPB. 
Background On XX/XX/XXXX, I entered the XXXX to with respect to a XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Lease states in pertinent part ( emphasis supplied ) : 3. Other Charges ( not part of your scheduled payment ) Disposition fee ( if you do not purchase the vehicle and we do not waive the fee under Section 13 ) : {$390.00} 31 Option to Buy the Vehicle. You have an option to buy the vehicle .... If this is a monthly payment lease, the price to buy the vehicle before the start of the last monthly period is ( 1 ) the price to buy the vehicle disclosed in Section 9, plus ( 2 ) the base monthly payment times the number of payments not yet due, minus ( 3 ) any unearned rent charge figured by the Actual Method ( see Section 41, based on the number of full monthly periods between early end and scheduled end. 
The only mechanism in the contract for the lessee to purchase the vehicle under Section 3 is the purchase option of Section 31. Therefore, the reasonable construction of Section 3 is that the lessee does not have to pay the Disposition Fee if it exercises its option under Section 31 to buy the vehicle.

After I entered into the Lease, the value of the XXXX increased above the option exercise price specified in the Lease, due to the vehicle shortage caused by the XXXX lockdowns. 
In XXXX, halfway through my lease, the XXXX XXXX dealership in XXXX, Michigan offered to exercise my option to purchase the vehicle, with the result that they would own the XXXX and I would be out from the lease without cost in their words. I agreed and to my knowledge and belief, the dealership purchased the vehicle from Ally, exercising my option under Section 31 of the LeasXXXX. 
At that time, the Lease was in full effect. There is no allegation that I had defaulted under the Lease. Neither Ally nor I had given any notice of termination to the other. In fact, Ally continued to deduct the monthly lease payment from my checking account after the transaction.

Approximately one month later, Ally refunded my final lease payment, which Ally had deducted from my checking account during the pendency of the dealerships purchase. 
XXXX years later, in XXXX, Ally began collections efforts to recover its so-called Disposition Fee under Section XXXX of the lease. 
Analysis Under Lease, I have no obligation to pay Disposition Fee if I purchase the vehicle by exercising the option of Section 31.

This is exactly what happened. I assigned my option under Section 31 to the Jeep dealership, which exercised my option to purchase the vehicle in my stead, thus ending my lease obligation to Ally with no obligation on my part to pay the Disposition Fee.

In its collection efforts, insists that its sale to the dealer was not pursuant to my purchase option but rather was some other type of wholesale disposition, as if the vehicle had come off the Lease and Ally had been burdened with the costs of disposition.

This is nonsense because this transaction was initiated during the term of the Lease not after its conclusion. Ally was certainly free to sell the vehicle during the Lease, but the Lease and my exclusive rights of possession would have remained intact. In other words, Ally could not undertake some wholesale disposition ( its words ) of the vehicle during my Lease and cart off the vehicle to the new owner while I was fully performing my payment allegations under the Lease.

The only mechanism in the Lease for Ally to sell the vehicle during the Lease and thereby terminate the Lease is the exercise by me of my purchase option. This is precisely what happened.

Ally may argue that the option right is personal to me and that I could not assign it to the dealership. Assuming that to be true, Ally could have declined to sell the vehicle to my assignee, the dealership. But Ally did not do this. Instead, it proceeded with the sale and thus waived any objection that it might have raised at the time. 
My characterization of the sale ( and the ultimate result that I have no obligation to pay the Disposition Fee ) is also consistent with the commercial intentions of the parties. The Disposition Fee compensates Ally for the time and trouble disposing of used and depreciated vehicles after they come off lease. When, instead, a lessee exercises the option to buy the vehicle during the lease, Ally has no disposition expenses and therefore does not ( as a matter of the terms of the Lease and its business practice ) charge the Disposition Fee. This is what happened in this matter except that instead of me exercising the purchase right, the dealership exercised it in my stead.

Conclusion For purposes of Section 3, the purchase of the vehicle by my dealership is a purchase by me, and accordingly I am not liable to Ally for payment of the Disposition Fee.

My ask is that Ally withdraw its claim for the Disposition Fee and retract any adverse information that it has posted to my credit history.

complaint_what_happened:
XX/XX/year> From : XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX Re : BMW Lease XXXX To : BMW Financial Services CC : Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) On XX/XX/year>, I called BMW FS to obtain a payoff quote for my lease of a XXXX BMW XXXX XXXX while I was in a XXXX Dealership looking to trade in this BMW to purchase a new car. I was transferred to a representative, who informed me the payoff amount was {$100000.00}. No restriction or limitation on paying off the vehicle were mentioned during this call besides the dollar amount. Utilizing this quoted dollar amount, I traded this vehicle into a XXXX Dealership as part of the purchase of a new vehicle. The XXXX Dealership offered me {$100000.00} for the vehicle, and I provide the XXXX Dealership a check for {$9900.00} to makeup for the negative equity. The XXXX Dealership then cut a check for {$100000.00} to BMWFS for the payoff. 
Subsequently, XX/XX/year>, I received a letter from BMW Financial Services ( BMWFS ) dated XX/XX/year> stating, in summary, that BMWFS had received a payoff from a third-party dealership, that they would return the payoff received by mail to the original sender, and that they would only accept a payoff from myself or a BMW Center . I called BMWFS Customer Service on XX/XX/year> to inquire as Section 30 Purchase Option of the lease agreement made no reference of such a restriction. After many minutes on hold, the representative pointed to Section 36 Assignment of the agreement as the controlling section for this restriction. When asked about options, the representative stated I could personally buy the vehicle not involving the dealer. I pointed out that the dealer was essentially acting as my agent in this transaction but that didnt matter. I then ask whether I had to pay in cash from a checking account or whether I could obtain a loan for the purchase as I dont have the full amount of funds available to do so on my own. The representative stated I could obtain a loan for the purchase, and stated that BMWFS worked with XXXX. The representative could transfer me to them to work on obtaining a loan. After obtaining a loan and purchasing the vehicle through XXXX, I would be free to do whatever I wanted with the vehicle, including transferring it to the dealership to whom the vehicle was traded in. 
On XX/XX/year> I called BWMFS and spoke with XXXX to inquire about the return of the check as XXXX ) neither the dealership nor I had received the check back and XXXX ) I learned from the dealership that the check had actually cleared and had been paid out of their bank account. BMWFS advised me that they deposited the check into their account on XXXX/XXXX/204, that they would hold the funds for 15 business days, and issue a refund check via mail no earlier than XX/XX/year>. I had asked why they deposited the check if they werent going to accept it, and she stated that it was how their lockbox process worked. I stated I and the dealership needed the funds urgently to make other arrangements to payoff the vehicle but she stated there was no way to expedite it. I suggested that since they deposited the check and didnt advise me on the phone about no third party payoffs when I called for XXXX that they could change course and accept the funds. XXXX said they would not as it was laid out in the lease agreement that they would not accept third party funds. I asked XXXX where it was in the lease agreement, and referred her to Section 30 Purchase Option which made no such reference She said Its vague, but its in there. I asked her to point to where it said that, and she again could not point out that language of not accepting third party payoffs. Instead, she referred to Section 36 Assignment and said that that is what that section meant. I asked to speak with someone who had the authority to make a decision on whether to accept the funds and XXXX said there was no one else she could transfer me to that had decision authority. I further asked if I or the dealership who sent in the funds would receive interest on the {$100000.00} while they held it for three weeks and she said no. 
Unfair, Deceptive or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ) It is my belief that the sequence and details of the events laid out above constitute Unfair Acts or Practices. Consumers, including myself, do not walk around with copies of lease agreements in their hands. When I called BMWFS Customer Service while at a dealership and asked for a payoff quote, not having access to important information ( i.e. that third party dealership payoffs were not accepted ) hindered my decision making ability and harmed me. Not being provided this information when obtaining a payoff via phone deprived me of important information to avoid injury. While BMWFS may say they subsequently emailed additional payoff details and restrictions to my email ( and they did ), this came too late. 
It is also my belief that BMWFSs act of accepting a check for {$100000.00}, depositing it in their account, then immediately advising the borrower that they wont accept the funds, and holding any refund for 15 business days ( 21 calendar days ) is abusive. BMWs process of accepting a check via automated lockbox and then layering on an after-the-fact review of said items where they choose to not accept the funds causes me harm. I am unable to remedy this situation because BMWFS is holding the funds for XXXX weeks before issuing a refund. BMWFS benefits from having these funds on their balance sheet for XXXX weeks, while I and the dealership from whom the funds are derived are further harmed by XXXX ) not being able to remedy the situation independently from BMW and XXXX ) not earning interest on the funds. BMWFS could choose to operate a payoff process that reviews items first for what they deem to be acceptable funds, and then return an unprocessed check to an issuer/consumer it they dont accept it. Instead, they choose to operate in a reverse order of accept funds, question the funds latera process that harms consumers. 
It is also my belief that BMFS is profiting from these abusive acts through their partnership with. XXXX for instance charges loan origination fees of {$390.00} for car loans originated through them. The fact that BMWFS refers consumers to XXXX when BMW consciously refuses to accept payoff funds from a third party dealership seems to benefit BMWFS and their partner while harming consumers. While BMWFS states they will not accept payoff funds from a third-party dealership, they will however accept payoff funds from a third party loan provider such as a XXXX It seems from whom BWMFS decides to accept third party funds for payoffs from is capricious and arbitrary. 
Finally, the lease agreement either is, or borders on deceptive. As admitted by BMWFS Representative XXXX during a phone call on XX/XX/year>, the payoff section of the lease agreement makes no reference to a prohibition on a payoff by a third party. BMWFS Representative stated the lease agreement on this topic was Vague, but its in there. Such a material point should be explicitly mentioned in the appropriate section on payoffs in the agreement ; instead, it appears to be materially omitted. BMWFS then must rely on daisy-chaining numerous sections together using legalese language to come to the finding they did on the meaning of the payoff section of the agreement. 
Ask My ask is that BMWFS, considering the above, accept the payoff funds already in their positions to payoff the lease agreement.

On XX/XX/year>, I sold a record on XXXX, an online marketplace, with PayPal as the payment processor. The buyer listed his shipping address in NY, United States. This discrepancy in addresses creates a loophole that can be exploited by dishonest buyers. 

I am concerned that the buyer may have deliberately used two different addresses to exploit PayPals policies, potentially enabling him to claim non-receipt of the item and request a refund, even though the item was delivered. This situation leaves me vulnerable to losing both the item and the payment, with no protection from PayPal, despite following the instructions provided on XXXX. 

PayPals strict policy of requiring sellers to ship only to the address listed in the PayPal transaction details, without consideration of legitimate discrepancies, essentially allows buyers to manipulate the system and obtain goods for free. This not only results in significant financial losses for sellers but also undermines trust in online transactions. 

I believe that this loophole in PayPals policy facilitates fraudulent activity and leaves honest sellers unprotected. I am filing this complaint to bring attention to this issue and to seek resolution, as well as to advocate for changes in PayPals policies that would better protect sellers from such exploitation.

product: Money transfer, virtual currency, or money service
complaint_what_happened:
On XX/XX/XXXX I authorized Capital One Bank [ CO ] to wire funds in the amount of {$24000.00} from my CO account to an account at XXXX XXXX XXXX [ XXXX or XXXX ]. This was the direct result of unsolicited fraudulent activity and specific instructions received over the Internet and telephone from an unknown person posing as a Capital One Bank fraud investigator. The very next day Saturday, XXXX XXXX I telephoned Capital Ones Account Activity office to report the suspected fraudulent transaction and to request that the wire transfer be cancelled. Instead of taking immediate action, the CO agent advised that I would have to call back on Monday, because the bank could not take any action with respect to canceling a wire transfer on Saturday or Sunday. I objected and said that I thought immediate action by CO was necessary because wire transfers transfer funds very quickly ; however, the CO agent only repeated that my request should be made on Monday. 

On Monday XXXX XXXX at XXXX XXXX  [ ET ] I again telephoned the CO Account Activity office and reported the fraudulent transaction on XXXX ; and I requested the immediate cancellation of my {$24000.00} wired to XXXX XXXX [ XXXX ]. Later in a phone call that same day or the following day a CO agent advised me that on XXXX XXXX at XXXX XXXX an electronic request was sent to XXXX wire office requesting the return of my wired funds because of suspected fraud. 

During the next 10 months I made numerous and frequent inquires to both CO and XXXX about the return of my funds. Finally on or about XX/XX/XXXX CO advised me that XXXX had responded saying that there were no funds available for return from the customers account. No further explanation was provided as to why my funds were not available at the time COs return request received on XX/XX/XXXX. My further requests to CO and XXXX for additional information were unsuccessful. 

On XX/XX/XXXX my local law enforcement agency, XXXX XXXX, SC Sheriffs Office, served an evidence subpoena upon XXXX  requesting detailed information about its handling of my funds wired on XX/XX/XXXX, and also information about any other transactions in that XXXX receiving account. On XX/XX/XXXX XXXX responded with detailed information showing that within the 3-day period from XX/XX/XXXX to XX/XX/XXXX three [ 3 ] separate wires of funds totaling {$110000.00} were received into that same XXXX  account, as follows : a wire from one other victim [ hereafter referred to as Victim 1 ' ] on XXXX XXXX in the amount of {$47000.00} ; and a second wire on XXXX XXXX in the amount of {$47000.00} from that same Victim 1 ; and a third wire from me [ hereafter sometimes referred to as Victim 2 ' ] also on XXXX XXXX in the amount of {$24000.00}. XXXX stated that those three wires were the only deposits received before that customers account was first frozen and then later closed. 

XXXX stated that on XXXX XXXX it thereafter received a Letter of Indemnity [ previously referred to as a Hold Request ] from Victim 1s bank before it received the Letter of Indemnity from Capital One in connection with my wired funds. Thereafter on XXXX XXXX and XXXX, XXXX XXXX returned funds totaling {$70000.00} to Victim 1s bank, which amount represented all remaining funds in the its customers closed account. As a result of those returns there were no funds remaining for XXXX to return to CO in connection with its request for the return of my funds. 

XXXX advised the Sheriffs investigator that Letters of Indemnity [ LOI ] are handled on a first-come, first-served basis in other words, whichever bank gets the LOI submitted first gets access to the money left in the suspect account. Accordingly, XXXX returned all the remaining funds to Victim 1 's bank and nothing to CO [ Victim 2 ]. Information in the XXXX report does not include details about the precise times of receipt of these separate LOIs from CO and XXXX. I have requested that information from XXXX, but it has not been provided. 

From the facts presented above, it seems clear that if Capital One had taken action to immediately send its Hold Request or LOI to XXXX when I first telephoned CO on Saturday XX/XX/XXXX to report the fraud incident, there would have been a very different outcome. COs return request/LOI for my wired funds would have been received substantially before the LOI was received from Victim 1 's bank on XX/XX/XXXX. Then pursuant to XXXX  first- come, first-served procedure, it is clear there would have been sufficient funds in its customers account for XXXX to return the full amount of {$24000.00} to CO for my benefit. 

Conclusion Based on the above information and analysis, I believe Capital One negligently failed in its duty to take immediate action on XX/XX/XXXX, as I requested, to request the return of my funds wired to XXXX XXXX on the previous day. That negligence directly resulted in XXXX actions several days later to return all the available funds to Victim 1 's bank. Accordingly, Capital One should be held responsible for the return of my {$24000.00}. In addition, CO should pay me interest at the same rate that those funds would have earned if they had been returned by XXXX on XXXX XX/XX/XXXX and immediately re-deposited into my CO Performance Savings Account.
